Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m glad we have this time together.  
I’m Dr. Bennett, a perinatal mental-health specialist. Over the next few minutes we’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply a set of 10 questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays confidential within our care team. My only goal is to make sure you feel heard and supported.

I’ll ask each question conversationally—just tell me what feels closest to your experience over the past seven days. Ready to start?

1. In the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, even when caring for the baby?

I can still laugh sometimes—maybe once or twice this week—but it feels like it takes more effort than it used to. Most of the time I’m just too tired or distracted by worrying about the baby to find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I can still laugh, but it’s not as easy or natural as before. I’ll chuckle if my partner makes a joke or if the baby does something cute, yet it feels kind of forced—like I have to remind myself to enjoy the moment instead of just feeling it right away.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I still plan little things—like taking the baby for a walk or having coffee with a friend—but the excitement isn’t there. I do them mostly because I “should,” not because I’m actually looking forward to them.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that bothered him, or I wasn’t holding him the “right” way. Rationally I know babies just cry, but I still catch myself wondering what I did to cause it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure he feels too warm—or too cool—or his breathing sounds “off.” I check on him constantly, even when there’s nothing wrong. It’s like I can’t shut off the “what-if” thoughts.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-blown panic, but a couple of times this week I’ve had that sudden rush of fear—like when the baby made a weird squeak at night. My chest got tight, I felt shaky, and I had to stand up and pace the hallway until I’d checked him three times and convinced myself he was fine.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes... a few nights this week I’ve lain in bed thinking, “How am I going to keep doing this every day?” It’s not that anything huge went wrong—just the constant cycle of feeding, changing, trying to soothe him, plus the housework piling up. I feel like I’m always one step behind, and it wears me out.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly “unhappy,” more like my mind won’t settle. I’ll finally get the baby down, crawl into bed exhausted, and then lie there running through everything I might have missed—did I sterilize the bottles, is the onesie warm enough, will he wake up in an hour? It takes me ages to drift off, and even then I wake at every little sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel that way some of the time—maybe three or four days this week. It’s not all day long, but there’ll be a moment, especially in the late afternoon when I’m really tired, where I just feel heavy and teary. It passes if I get a little rest or talk to my partner, but it keeps popping up.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

No, I haven’t actually cried. I’ve felt on the edge of tears a couple of times—like when the baby wouldn’t settle and I couldn’t figure out why—but the tears never quite came. I mostly just felt exhausted and frustrated instead.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. My baby needs me, and I want to be here for him.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening (EPDS-10)

**Chief concerns endorsed:**
- Anhedonia / reduced pleasure (Q2)
- Excessive self-blame / guilt (Q3)
- Daily, intrusive “what-if” anxiety and physiologic arousal without clear precipitant (Q4, Q5)
- Feeling overwhelmed and unable to cope with routine infant care/household tasks (Q6)
- Sleep-onset difficulty linked to racing, worry-filled thoughts (Q7)
- Episodic sad/miserable mood 3–4 days/week (Q8)

**Patterns noted:**
- Persistent worry and hyper-vigilance regarding infant safety
- Afternoon “low” mood when fatigued
- Functional impairment (tasks “pile up,” sense of “always behind”)

**Screening significance:**  
Responses suggest clinically elevated symptoms consistent with postpartum anxiety and possible minor depressive symptoms; however, no anhedonia on Q1 and no crying spells (Q9) or self-harm ideation (Q10) were endorsed.

**Safety:** Denies thoughts of self-harm (Q10). No current safety concern identified.

**Next step:** Continue with standardized scoring and consider further perinatal mood/anxiety evaluation.
